overview: This file documents uncertainty over the South Manchuria Railway Company’s proposed Showa Steel Works in mid-1930. A detailed despatch from the American consul at Dairen explains the plan to expand Anshan’s pig-iron output and manufacture billets and sheet bars for finishing in Japan, but emphasizes delays caused by the Hamaguchi government’s fiscal policy, low world steel prices, customs duties, subsidy requirements, and unresolved political questions. A subsequent cross-reference sheet and attached report extract show that officials were considering Shin Gishu in colonial Korea instead of Anshan, subject partly to the suitability of Tashito as a harbor, while abandonment of the enterprise remained possible.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 118 from Dairen on the Showa Steel Works
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the progress, obstacles, and uncertain prospects of the South Manchuria Railway Company’s proposed Showa Steel Works.
subfiles.summary: The South Manchuria Railway Company proposed increasing annual output at Anshan from 225,000 to 400,000 tons, retaining 140,000 tons as pig iron and converting the balance into billets and sheet bars for finishing in Japan. Although a new company with subscribed capital of ¥100 million had been incorporated and roughly $3 million in German machinery ordered, the project remained stalled after the fall of the Tanaka Cabinet. Gōdō blamed politics for the delay, while Sengoku questioned whether the works could be profitable at prevailing steel prices and criticized the earlier administration for proceeding before tariff, customs, and subsidy questions had been resolved. The machinery was lying on the Dairen wharves while the Japanese government considered whether to proceed or abandon the scheme.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Neville’s report on the proposed steel-works site
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a report from Japan concerning the possible establishment of the Showa Steel Works at Shin Gishu rather than Anshan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a report numbered 219 from Japan, attributed to Neville and dated August 1, 1930. Its abstract states that the proposed works might be established at Shin Gishu in Chosen instead of Anshan in Manchuria and notes that the entire project might still be abandoned; a copy is identified as attached.

subfiles.title: Attached report extract on Shin Gishu versus Anshan
subfiles.about: Describes the apparent shift toward Shin Gishu as the site of the proposed Showa Steel Works and the official interests behind that choice.
subfiles.summary: Although Anshan had appeared to be the likely site in June, reports at the end of July indicated a sharp reversal in favor of Shin Gishu in Chosen, while rumors of complete abandonment persisted. Sengoku apparently remained the principal senior advocate for Anshan, whereas the foreign minister, finance minister, and governor-general of Chosen favored locating the works in Japanese-controlled territory, partly because this would facilitate tariff exemptions and government bounties. Selection of Shin Gishu depended on whether nearby Tashito could serve as a satisfactory harbor, and Sengoku returned to Dairen for further investigation after consulting engineers in Tokyo.

interest: The file is valuable for showing how a major industrial project was shaped not simply by engineering considerations but by cabinet politics, colonial geography, tariffs, export duties, subsidies, and depressed world steel prices. It preserves unusually concrete figures for intended production, capitalization, and machinery costs while also recording disagreement between Gōdō’s confidence and Sengoku’s skepticism. The attached report captures a rapid change in policy from Anshan toward Shin Gishu and reveals how the jurisdictional advantages of colonial Korea and the suitability of a nearby harbor could determine the location of heavy industry within Japan’s empire.
